newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE white sugar thin, awaits break of NY range.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE white sugar thin, awaits break of NY range.

text.p: White sugar futures resumed their gentle downward correction after this week's fund-led gains but traders said London was wary of moving too sharply until New York broke its current range.

"People are sitting back for the time being seeing how the dust settles," said one trader, referring to the concerted fund buying earlier in the week which drove benchmark October up to a new life of contract high of $330.20.
Traders said the focus of the market at the moment was on raws with a stalemate arising as gains racked up from fund buying were capped by trade and producer selling.
"London is hanging onto the tails of whatever New York does at the moment, there doesn't appear to be any real movement going on in the whites," the trader said.

New York's October contract has traded two consecutive inside sessions compared with Tuesday's rally to a peak of 11.65 cents/lb. That day's low was 11.31. In London, a handful of trade and commission house players were cited as leading the thin session.
But although October stood 60 cents higher at an intraday high of $328.50 by 1110 GMT, the position was trapped in a tight range of just $1.00.
December was untraded and volume reached 380 lots.
Technical analysts said the London market looked poised to make further gains in the coming sessions.
"We think it only a matter of time before $330.20 breaks and we expect support at $325.00 and $321.70 to underpin gains," said Adrian Haylor, analyst at Sucden.
October also dominated trading in Paris and stood $1.20 higher at $328.20. December was up $1.00 at $322.50 and Matif volume amounted to 344 lots.
Nothing was traded on the lesser-quality 100 ICUMSA white sugar market.

There was little fundamental news to spur sentiment. Ukraine revised down its forecast for the 1997 sugar beet crop to 27 million tonnes from 30-31 million tonnes. China imported 360,000 tonnes of sugar in the six months of 1997, down by 35.6 percent from the same period in 1996. --Jeremy Smith, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8064
